images.caption:
George V and his Prime Ministers at the 1926 Imperial Conference.  The conference was the seventh Imperial Conference held amongst the Prime Ministers of the dominions of the British Empire. It was held in London from 19 October to 22 November 1926.  It was notable as the conference that produced the Balfour Declaration, which established the principle that the dominions are all equal in status, and not subordinate to the United Kingdom.
George V (seated, centre) with Rt. Hon. Stanley Baldwin (United Kingdom; seated left), Rt. Hon. W.L. Mackenzie King (Canada; seated right). Standing Rt. Hon. Walter Stanley Monroe (Newfoundland), Rt. Hon. Gordon Coates (New Zealand), Rt. Hon. Stanley Bruce (Australia), Rt. Hon. J. B. M. Hertzog (Union of South Africa) and W.T. Cosgrave (Irish Free State). All are wearing alternative court dress with decorations; Coates is wearing his service medals in miniature (Military Cross and Bar, 1914-15 Star, British War Medal, Victory Medal); Bruce is wearing his service medals in miniature (Military Cross, 1914-15 Star, British War Medal, Victory Medal, Croix de Guerre); Cosgrave is wearing the star and sash of the Knight Grand Cross of the Order of Pope Pius IX; George V is wearing medals in miniature and the star, riband and garter as a Knight of the Order of the Garter; Mackenzie King is wearing the collar badge and miniature medal of the Companion of the Order of St Michael and St George.
images.alt:

images.caption:
Four watercolors showing dwellings in Bluefields on the Mosquito Coast (also Mosquito Shore), then a British protectorate. They are the work of a traveler who was in Bluefields in July 1845.
The same year these watercolors were done, the new Miskito boy king and his guardian, the British Agent, settled in Bluefields, which had been chosen as the "capital" of the Miskito Coast. German Moravian Church colonists settled there early in 1847 but nearly all had left three years later.

 "Bluefields is the capital of Mosquitia. It is situated on the river and lagoon of the same name. In the midst of the palms bordering the river is the residence of the king, and his English tutor or guardian, over which floats the British flag. At some distance from this is the House of Justice, which is under the Mosquitia flag." (Belize newspaper article from the late 1840s)

images.caption:
The English translation presents the monologue backwards, as w:en:traditional Japanese writing went from right to left instead:
Japan: “I must censure your rudeness.”
Hawaii: “Oh, Uncle! Please help me.”
America: “All right, you may stay in my home.”
England: “Oh, no! Mr. America must not take off this boy.”
After the w:en:overthrow of the Hawaiian monarchy in January 1893, the w:en:United States was considering annexing w:en:Hawaii.
In the late 1890s, w:enAmerican political cartoons illustrated w:en:manifest destiny, or America's geopolitical and colonial expansion. The United States considered annexing Hawaii, w:en:Cuba, w:en:Puerto Rico, and the w:en:Philippines.
Cartoons portrayed the territories as children with dark skin, grass skirts, nappy hair, and bare feet. w:en:Uncle Sam personified the United States, their supposed w:en:warden.

w:en:Political cartoons expressed, shaped, reinforced, and reflected social, political, and racial conditions of a society. Therefore, newspapers used cartoons as propaganda to shape public opinion. As mirrors to public knowledge, cartoons showed what the public knew.

images.filename: An early Canada stamp showing the extent of the British Empire (24772466501).jpg
images.caption: 'We hold a vaster empire than beer'! An amusing jingle on an early Canadian postal stamp dating back to 1898. This is a large blow-up of that postage stamp in the Canada War Museum which shows the extent of the British Empire back then. Vast swathes of Canada were held by the British while other stretches were held by the French. Ottawa city itself is divided into the British half and the French half. (Ottawa, Canada, June 2015)

images.caption: Acorn Street is a historic and picturesque cobblestone street located in the renowned Beacon Hill neighborhood of Boston, Massachusetts, USA. This charming street has become a beloved attraction, drawing visitors from near and far. Acorn Street is characterized by its well-preserved row houses, constructed in brick and stone, which exude a timeless elegance. The street's gas lamps, quaint flower boxes, and narrow layout create a nostalgic ambiance, evoking the charm of the 19th century. Particularly during the autumn season, Acorn Street's beauty reaches new heights, as the vibrant foliage of the trees that line the street transforms into a stunning tapestry of red and orange hues. Although Acorn Street is a popular destination for tourists, its appeal extends beyond its visual splendor. The street provides a glimpse into Boston's rich history and serves as a living testament to the city's architectural heritage. Whether strolling along the cobblestones or admiring the captivating facades, a visit to Acorn Street offers a truly immersive experience in the heart of Boston's cultural tapestry.
